                  <ns0:p n="5">5 ¶ And the Philistines gathered themselves together to fight with Israel, thirty thousand cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rets <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This number seems incredible to Infidels. To whom it may be sufficient to reply, That it is far more rational to ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />knowledge a mistake in him that Copied out the Sacred Text in such Numeral or Historical passages, wherein the Doctrine of Faith and Good Life is not directly concerned, than upon such a pretence to question the Truth and Divinity of the Holy Scriptures, which are so fully Attested, and evidently Demonstrated.                   <ns0:p n="13">13 And Samuel said to Saul, Thou hast done foolishly <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">In that very thing wherein thou thinkest thou hast done wisely and politickly, in disobeying my express Command upon a pretended necessity, or reason of State.</ns0:note>: thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD thy God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Not one<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly upon common grounds, as thou art his Creature, and one of his People; but in a special manner, who hath confer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red peculiar Favours and Honours upon thee: which is an aggravation of thy sin.</ns0:note>, which he commanded thee: for now would the LORD have established thy kingdom upon Israel for ever <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">

And there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore God might well promise the Kingdom to <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> because at that time, and before, he foresaw that <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> would by his disobedience forfeit that promise, and that he would take the forfeiture, and transfer the Kingdom to <ns0:hi>Iudah.</ns0:hi>

                        <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> First, What was <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s sin? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Either, First, That <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> Invaded the Priests Office, and Offered the Sacrifice himself: which is not probable, both because he had Priests with him, and among others an eminent one, <ns0:hi>Ahiah, chap.</ns0:hi> 14. 3. and therefore had no occasion nor pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tence for that presumption. Or rather, Secondly, That <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> did not wait the full time for <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi>'s coming; for that is the thing which God commanded, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 10. 8. and the breach of this command is the onely thing for which <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> makes an Apology, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11, 12. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Secondly, Why did God so severely punish <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> for so small an offence, and that occasioned by great necessity, and done with an honest intention? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> First, Men are very incompetent <ns0:hi>Iudges</ns0:hi> of Gods Judgments, because they see but very little, either of the Majesty of the offended God, or of the hainous nature and aggravations of the Offence. For instance, men see no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing but <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s outward act, which seems small; but God saw with how wicked a mind and heart he did this, with what Rebellion against the Light of his own Conscience, as his own words imply; with what gross infidelity and distrust of Gods Providence; with what contempt of Gods Autho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity, and Justice, and many other wicked principles and mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions of his heart, unknown to men. Besides, God clearly saw all that wickedness that yet lay hid in his heart, and foresaw all his other Crimes; and therefore had far more grounds for his Sentence against him, than we can imagine. Secondly, God doth sometimes punish small sins severely, and that for divers weighty reasons, as that all men may see what the least sin deserves, and how much they owe to Gods free and rich Mercy, for passing by their great Offences; and what need they have not to indulge themselves in any small sin, as men are very prone to do, upon vain presumptions of Gods Mercy, whereby they are easily and commonly drawn on to hainous Crimes; and for many other reasons: so that some such instances of Gods severity, are necessary Discipline and Caution to all mankind in the present and future Ages; and therefore there is far more of mercy and kindness in such actions, than of rigour and harshness, since this is but parti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cular to one Person, and the other is an universal good. Thirdly, It must be remembred, that the Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> and of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> was now in its Infancy; and that this was the first command which he received from God. And it hath been ever held a piece of Wisdom in all Law-givers, severe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly to punish the first Violations of their Laws, to secure their Honour and Obedience, and to affright and caution Offenders for the future. And accordingly God dealt with <ns0:hi>Cain</ns0:hi> the first Murderer; with <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> for their first Idolatty with the Calf; with the first miscarriage of the Priests, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 10. 1. with the first profaner of the Sabbath, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 15. 32. with the first gross Hypocrites in the Christian Church, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 5. 5, 10. And therefore it is neither strange nor unjust, if he deal with <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> after the same manner, and upon the same grounds. Fourthly, Though God threaten <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> with the loss of his Kingdom for this sin; yet it is not improbable, that there was a tacit condition implied, as is usual in such cases, as <ns0:hi>Ionah</ns0:hi> 3. 4. to wit, if he did not heartily repent of this and of all his sins; for the full, and final, and peremptory Sentence of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s rejection, is plainly ascribed to another cause, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 15. 11, 23, 26, 28, 29. and till that second Offence, neither the Spirit of the Lord departed from him, nor was <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nointed in his stead, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 13, 14.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:228" />19 ¶ Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This was a Politick course of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> which also other Nations have used. So the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> took away their Smiths, 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 24. 14. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 24. 1. and 29. 2. And <ns0:hi>Porsenna</ns0:hi> obliged the <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> by Covenant, That they should use no Iron but in the Tillage of their Lands.</ns0:note>: (for the Philistines said, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">We must take them away.</ns0:note> Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 But all the Israelites went down to the Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listines <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not to the Land of the <ns0:hi>Philistines,</ns0:hi> for it is not said so, and that was too remote; but to the Stations and Garisons which the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> yet retained in several parts of <ns0:hi>Israels</ns0:hi> Land, though <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi>'s Authority had so far over-awed them, that they durst not give the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> much Disturbance. In these, therefore, the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> kept all the Smiths; and here they allowed them the exercise of their Art for the uses here following.</ns0:note> to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Yet they had <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Hebr.</ns0:hi> a file with mouths.</ns0:note> a file for the mattocks, and for the coulters, and for the forks, and for the axes <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">So the sense is, They allowed them some small helps to make their Mattocks, and in some sort to serve their present use. But these words may be otherwise Translated, and are so by some Learned, both Ancient and Modern, Translators; thus, <ns0:hi>Therefore the mouths or edges of the mattocks, and coulters,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>were dull</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>blunt.</ns0:hi> Or rather thus, <ns0:hi>When</ns0:hi> (Heb. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> put for <ns0:hi>when,</ns0:hi> as the Particle, <ns0:hi>and,</ns0:hi> is sometimes rendred, as <ns0:hi>Mar.</ns0:hi> 15. 25.) <ns0:hi>the mouths</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>edges of the mattocks,</ns0:hi> &c. <ns0:hi>were blunt.</ns0:hi> So this passage very well agrees both with the foregoing and following words; and the whole sence of the place is in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tirely thus, They <ns0:hi>went to the Philistines to sharpen their shares, and mattocks, and coulters, and axes, when they were blunt, and</ns0:hi> (which was more strange, They were forced to go to them, even) <ns0:hi>to sharpen their goads.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to set.</ns0:note> to sharpen the goads.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 So it came to pass in the day of battel, that there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people, that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with Saul and Jonathan <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> How could the <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> smite either the Garison of the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> above, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. or the Host of the <ns0:hi>Ammonites, Chap.</ns0:hi> 11. 11. without Arms? And when they had Conquer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed them, Why did they not take away their Arms, and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve them to their own use? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> 1. This want of Swords and Spears is not affirmed concerning all <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> but is re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strained unto those 600. who were with <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ionathan?</ns0:hi> whom God by his Providence might suffer to be without those Arms, that the glory of the following Victory might be wholly ascribed to God; as for the very same reason God would have but 300 men left with <ns0:hi>Gideon,</ns0:hi> and those Armed onely with Trumpets, and Pitchers, and Lamps, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 7. There were no doubt a considerable number of Swords and Spears among the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> but they generally hid them, as now they did their Persons, from the <ns0:hi>Philistines.</ns0:hi> And the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> had not yet attained to so great a power over them, as wholly to disarm them, but thought it suffici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ent to prevent the making of new Arms; knowing that the old ones would shortly be decayed, and useless. 2. There were other Arms more common in those times and places, than Swords and Spears; to wit, Bows and Arrows, and Slings and Stones; as appears from <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 20. 16. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1. 18, 22. 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 3. 25. 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 12. 1, 2. besides Clubs, and Instruments of Agriculture, which might easily be turned into weapons of War. 3. God so governed the Affairs of the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> that they had no great number of Swords, or Spears, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 5. 8. that so they might be kept in more de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pendence upon, and subjection unto God, wherein their safety and happiness consisted. And therefore, that famous Victory obtained against the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi>'s days, was not got by the Sword of Men, but onely by Thunder from Heaven, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 7. 10.</ns0:note>, but with Saul and with Jonathan his son was there found.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, standing Camp.</ns0:note> garison of the Philistines went out to the passage of Michmash <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">A place so called, because it was near to <ns0:hi>Michmash,</ns0:hi> and led towards <ns0:hi>Gibeah,</ns0:hi> which, it seems, they designed to Besiege; and in the mean time, to wast the adjoyning Country.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
